prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B028 rests on a simple, general mechanism: spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge or surface states. Kane and Mele wrote it as a minimal tight-binding model on graphene that can be analysed exactly, and the idea then carried over to three dimensions and to a general classification of band structures. It was a prediction confirmed in nature, by Molenkamp's HgTe edge-conductance measurement in 2007, and later by many independent groups in many materials. Six of eight members ranked it, four in their top three, and five of the six independently proposed exactly Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The field is about two decades old and textbook material, so the interpretation is stable. It extends the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and does not repeat it, because it concerns symmetry-protected band topology in real materials and not topological phase transitions in model systems.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction without which Molenkamp's experiment would not have been done, and none of them is in the credited names. The 3D strand (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy, and Hasan's ARPES on Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3) is excluded by the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio, even though many in the field would call it the more consequential half. The HgTe edge conductance also fell short of perfect quantisation, and practical applications are still modest, so a sceptic can call this a conceptual prize with a thin experimental half. A prize built on a different slate, with Hasan for the 3D case, would be at least as defensible.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B028 first as a new class of quantum matter whose predictions match measured spectra, and he flags that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is defensible but not unique, given the absent Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 3D pioneers.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and with the caveat, and I would go slightly further on the caveat. Calling the trio not unique understates the 2D/3D split. The HgTe edge channel and the Bi-based surface states test the same Z2 mechanism in different dimensionality, and I read the Kane-Mele Z2 classification as the unifying step that makes both count as one discovery. That is why I keep Hasan as an alternative and not a co-laureate. Where I differ is on how comfortable we should be with the missing theorists. I do not think an incomplete credit list is a reason to lower the rank, but we should write the citation narrowly enough that the omission is not a misstatement of history.

responses.point: Olsson puts B046 first as a tunable platform whose 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity observation is the decisive experiment, and she would credit Andrei's earlier STM work in place of Bistritzer.
responses.response: I rank B046 second and agree that it opened a field, but I disagree that the early flat-band STM observations carry the same weight as the transport discovery. Andrei's work saw twist-induced Van Hove singularities, whereas Jarillo-Herrero's group saw the correlated phases the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat band was expected to produce. I also dissent from calling recognition timely. The pairing mechanism is unresolved and the field is about eight years old, whereas the topological-insulator case has had fifteen years of confirmation. A twist-angle prize may come soon, but I would not put it ahead of B028 now. If the committee does go there, Bistritzer's exclusion is the weaker of the credit choices, because the continuum model is what made the magic angle a prediction and not a surprise.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on the strength of its strong-coupling physics and its role under superconducting processors, while admitting that proximity to the 2025 circuits prize and his own closeness to the field are concerns. He ranks B028 second with the same trio.
responses.response: I respect that Johansson raised his own proximity openly. My doubt on B035 is mainly about the novelty step, not about the quality of the work. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum behaviour in a circuit, and circuit QED is its natural continuation, so awarding both in consecutive years looks like one device family. Since he also puts B028 second with exactly my trio, I think the committee can accommodate both views by taking B028 now and leaving circuit QED for a later year. I would also ask him whether the Girvin and Huang omission, which he himself flags, damages the theory credit more than the missing names in B028 do.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because they open new observables (millimetre redshift, varying constants, geodesy) and a coming redefinition of the second, and he sees a clean two-name configuration.
responses.response: The attribution for B034 is cleaner than for B028, and I agree it is mature and independently confirmed. I put it below B028 because the physics question it answers is of a different kind. The magic-wavelength idea is a clever and original way to eliminate the light shift, but the discovery is a record in precision, and the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize already recognise the surrounding technology. I accept that a measurement-driven prize can be a better choice for this year, and I would put B034 as an alternative, not an afterthought. I would like him to say what new physics, not accuracy, the clocks have so far delivered.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube astrophysical neutrino discovery first as a clean clue from nature, mature and confirmed in several channels, but admits that a solo prize for Halzen leaves credit questions for a collaboration-scale result.
responses.response: This is outside my own field, and I take his physics case seriously. My difficulty is attribution, which is exactly the point he raises. A single name for a detector built by a large collaboration after AMANDA is a heavier credit problem than the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp slate, where at least the theory and the first experiment have identifiable authors. If the committee chooses B005 despite that, I would want a citation that recognises the discovery and not one person's leadership of a collaboration, and I would be uneasy if the supplied credited names cannot be extended. I did not rank it, so I defer to him on the instrument-side detail.

uncertainties: Whether a three-name slate can honestly cover both the 2D quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulator strands, or whether Hasan should replace Mele or Molenkamp.
Priority claims for Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Moore-Balents-Roy, which are outside the supplied names, and I cannot verify them here.
Whether the committee views topological insulators as sufficiently distinct from the 2016 prize and as more urgent than the younger twisted-graphene case.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have no known collaboration with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan or the other credited people. I only note that Johansson and Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment, which is an institutional fact and not a personal connection to any candidate.
